messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha Tane is a 35-year-old Māori woman, married and working as an accountant at a mid-sized firm in Auckland's financial district. She presented for treatment approximately eight months after being mugged on her way home from a late evening at the office. The assault occurred in a poorly lit side street she cut through regularly; a man came up quickly behind her, and it was the sound of his footsteps — rapid, closing — that she registered a half-second before he grabbed her shoulder from behind, spun her around, pressed something cold against her ribs, and demanded her bag. She remembers the metallic taste of fear flooding her mouth as she stood frozen, her body bent slightly backward the way he had wrenched her, her handbag stripped from her arm before he disappeared into the dark. The whole event lasted under a minute, but it remade her world entirely.

In the weeks that followed, Aroha found that the memory did not behave like other memories. When it returned — unbidden, at her desk, in the kitchen, during meetings — she did not merely recall the mugging; she tasted that cold metallic wash on her tongue again, and felt her torso twist backward into the same wrenched position she had been held in. The memory was so extreme, so total in its physical return, that she sometimes found herself unable to believe it had actually happened to her — it felt more like something she had witnessed than something she had lived. Yet the doubt offered no relief, because the body kept insisting otherwise. These intrusive, viscerally embodied memories reliably sharpened her sense of ongoing danger, leaving her in a state of physiological readiness that she could not talk herself out of. Even when her husband held her hand and told her she was safe, she found it impossible to believe him — the threat felt present and structural, not situational, and no amount of reassurance could penetrate it.

What frightened Aroha most, in the quieter moments of reflection, was what she had come to believe the mugging said about her. She was certain, at a level that felt like knowledge rather than opinion, that the event had happened because of the sort of person she was and because of the way she had acted — cutting through that street again, working late again, being careless again. This conviction that she was, in some essential way, the author of her own harm meant that the world's danger felt personally directed. She had come to believe the world was a dangerous place, and that she moved through it as someone who attracted its worst. These appraisals did not stay abstract; they fed directly back into her alertness, so that every environment she entered was scanned for threat. When a delivery arrived late at the office, she did not think "traffic" — she assumed something bad was unfolding. She could not relax even in her own home.

Aroha works in an open-plan office, and it is there that the tightest loops of her distress play out. Colleagues pass behind her workstation constantly, and the sound of footsteps approaching from behind — the very auditory signature of the assault — sends her rigid. In those moments, the threat floods back as certainty rather than fear, and she immediately begins dwelling on what she had done wrong that night, cycling through every decision that might have prevented it. If a colleague touched her shoulder unexpectedly to get her attention, she would dissociate deliberately, trying to blank out and leave her body, the only tool she had found that interrupted the sensation. But the rumination and dissociation that she used to manage these moments kept the memory raw and close, and when she emerged from a dissociative episode she often felt more convinced than before that she was fundamentally unsafe and fundamentally at fault. Her maladaptive attempts to cope quietly reinforced the very appraisals they were meant to quiet, and those appraisals in turn made her hypervigilant to the triggers that started the cycle again.

Over months, she began arriving at work before her colleagues and leaving last, rearranging her schedule to avoid the busy corridor. Relationships with her team became strained — she seemed distant, startled easily, and declined after-work gatherings. What finally brought her to seek help was her husband's quiet observation, one evening, that she no longer seemed to be living in their home so much as guarding it. She came to the first session hoping, above all, to stop feeling like a person to whom danger was inevitable — and afraid that she no longer knew how to believe she was safe.
